ranking.rationale: Age is a strong, semantically stable predictor of cholesterol-related outcomes and general health status across domains, with low risk of leakage or shortcut learning compared with diagnosis or survey-year features.
Diabetes/prediabetes status is a strong, semantically stable medical risk factor for cholesterol outcomes and should generalize better than demographic or year-based shortcuts.
Diabetes status is a strong, semantically stable predictor of cholesterol outcomes and complements age and prior diabetes history without relying on obvious domain-specific artifacts.

Hypertension is a stable cardiometabolic comorbidity that should remain predictive of cholesterol-related outcomes across domains, adding clinically meaningful signal beyond age, diabetes, and diabetes treatment while avoiding obvious site/year leakage.

Arthritis is a plausible stable health-status predictor of cholesterol-related outcomes and adds complementary clinical information beyond age, diabetes, and blood pressure history, while avoiding obvious domain or year leakage.

Kidney disease history is plausibly and stably related to cholesterol risk across domains, and adds direct clinical signal beyond the already selected age, diabetes, blood pressure, and comorbidity features.

Psoriasis is a chronic health condition that can add stable signal about metabolic and inflammatory risk without strongly encoding site/year/domain artifacts; it is more likely to generalize than demographics or survey-year proxies.

Education is a stable socioeconomic health proxy that can add predictive signal for cholesterol-related outcomes without being as domain-specific or leakage-prone as year, and it complements the already selected age, diabetes, blood pressure, and kidney-related features.

Gender is a broadly stable demographic predictor of cholesterol-related outcomes and can add signal beyond age, diabetes, blood pressure, kidney history, and education without being as domain-specific or leakage-prone as year or dialysis.

Marital status is a relatively stable socioeconomic/behavioral correlate of cholesterol-related health risk and can add predictive signal beyond age, sex, education, and chronic-condition indicators without being as domain-specific as year or birthplace.

Dialysis status is a clinically meaningful marker of severe kidney disease and related metabolic risk, so it should generalize better than year or birthplace while adding stable predictive signal beyond the already selected demographics and comorbidity indicators.

Country of birth is a relatively stable demographic/health-access proxy that can add predictive signal for cholesterol-related outcomes without directly encoding the split year; nhanes_year is more likely to capture domain shift and benchmark artifacts.
The year indicator can capture broad cohort- and survey-wave shifts that may remain predictive after accounting for demographics and comorbidities, and it is the only remaining candidate.
